content: Benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus, known as fibroids or myomas, are often asymptomatic. However, approximately one-third of women with fibroids experience symptoms severe enough to require treatment. For women who have completed childbearing, the standard treatment for symptomatic fibroids is hysterectomy, which involves the surgical removal of the uterus. For women who wish to preserve their uterus or desire future childbearing, myomectomy, the surgical removal of fibroids, is the preferred treatment. However, myomectomy is associated with the risk of significant bleeding, which can be life-threatening and may necessitate emergency blood transfusion. Understanding the effectiveness of interventions to reduce bleeding during myomectomy is critical for evidence-based clinical decision-making. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, safety, tolerability, and costs of various interventions designed to reduce blood loss during myomectomy. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing interventions to reduce blood loss with placebo or no treatment. The primary outcomes assessed were the amount of blood loss and the need for blood transfusion. The quality of evidence was evaluated using GRADE methodology. Eighteen RCTs involving 1,250 participants were included in the analysis. These studies were conducted in hospital settings across low-, middle-, and high-income countries. The following findings were reported: 1. Blood Loss Reduction: Vaginal misoprostol significantly reduced blood loss (2 RCTs, 89 women; mean difference [MD] -97.88 mL; moderate-quality evidence). Intramyometrial vasopressin showed a substantial reduction in blood loss (3 RCTs, 128 women; MD -245.87 mL; moderate-quality evidence). Intramyometrial bupivacaine combined with epinephrine reduced blood loss (1 RCT, 60 women; MD -68.60 mL; low-quality evidence). Intravenous tranexamic acid significantly decreased blood loss (1 RCT, 100 women; MD -243 mL; low-quality evidence). Gelatin-thrombin matrix was associated with a marked reduction in blood loss (1 RCT, 50 women; MD -545.00 mL; low-quality evidence). Intravenous ascorbic acid reduced blood loss (1 RCT, 102 women; MD -411.46 mL; low-quality evidence). Vaginal dinoprostone showed a reduction in blood loss (1 RCT, 108 women; MD -131.60 mL; low-quality evidence). Loop ligation of the myoma pseudocapsule reduced blood loss (1 RCT, 70 women; MD -305.01 mL; low-quality evidence). A fibrin sealant patch reduced blood loss (1 RCT, 70 women; MD -26.50 mL; low-quality evidence). A Foley catheter tied around the cervix reduced blood loss (1 RCT, 93 women; MD -240.70 mL; low-quality evidence). A polyglactin suture placed around both the cervix and infundibulopelvic ligament significantly reduced blood loss (1 RCT, 28 women; MD -1870.00 mL; low-quality evidence). There was no evidence of a significant effect on blood loss with oxytocin, morcellation, or temporary clipping of the uterine artery. 2. Need for Blood Transfusion: Vasopressin significantly reduced the need for blood transfusion (2 RCTs, 90 women; odds ratio [OR] 0.15; moderate-quality evidence). A tourniquet tied around the cervix reduced the need for transfusion (1 RCT, 98 women; OR 0.22; low-quality evidence). A tourniquet tied around both the cervix and infundibulopelvic ligament significantly reduced the need for transfusion (1 RCT, 28 women; OR 0.02; low-quality evidence). Gelatin-thrombin matrix reduced the need for transfusion (1 RCT, 100 women; OR 0.01; low-quality evidence). Dinoprostone reduced the need for transfusion (1 RCT, 108 women; OR 0.17; low-quality evidence). There was no evidence of a significant effect on the need for transfusion with misoprostol, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, ascorbic acid, loop ligation of the myoma pseudocapsule, or a fibrin sealant patch. There was insufficient data to assess the adverse effects and costs of the various interventions. In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence suggests that misoprostol and vasopressin may reduce bleeding during myomectomy. Low-quality evidence indicates that bupivacaine plus epinephrine, tranexamic acid, gelatin-thrombin matrix, ascorbic acid, dinoprostone, loop ligation, a fibrin sealant patch, a peri-cervical tourniquet, or a tourniquet tied around both the cervix and infundibulopelvic ligament may also reduce bleeding. There is no evidence to support the effectiveness of oxytocin, morcellation, or temporary clipping of the uterine artery in reducing blood loss. Further well-designed studies are needed to establish the effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness of these interventions.
